views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Proceed with a calibrated Section 301 tariff package aimed at Chinese industrial-policy and technology goods (the $30–60 billion range already under White House debate), not another global metals-style blast. Pair the announcement with a clear offer of talks on forced technology transfer, JV/equity caps, and discriminatory licensing, and keep investment restrictions and visa measures in reserve until they are legally tight. Do not roll back the newly signed 232 steel/aluminum duties yet, but stop widening them and use ally exemptions to rebuild a coalition for the China IP case.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is an opportunity, not an emergency. The underlying Chinese practices are real and costly — USTR’s 301 inquiry (opened after the 14 Aug 2017 memorandum) targets JV/equity-forced transfer, non-market licensing, state-directed acquisition of U.S. tech, and cyber-enabled IP theft; USCBC’s Sep 2017 filing said nearly 20% of member firms had been asked to transfer technology in three years, and Lighthizer has flagged Made in China 2025 as the industrial-policy core. The 8 Nov 2017 Beijing visit produced commercial MOUs and no structural IP concessions; China rejected 301 consultations as “irresponsible.” That is a genuine long-run threat to U.S. tech leadership, but it is not yet an existential or even high near-term shock: U.S. consumer sentiment is 101.4 (Mar 2018), industrial production is rising (102.2), CPI is contained, the goods deficit is large but not newly crisis-like (~$69.8bn in Mar), and VIX has settled near 18 after the February spike. China remains more goods-export exposed to the U.S. (U.S. imports from China still ~$38bn/month vs ~$12.7bn exports) with stable reserves (~$3.16tn) and a stronger yuan (~6.32), so the terrain favors using leverage.

Action should therefore be moderate escalation on the right instrument, not hold and not maximal war. Steel/aluminum 232 (signed 8 Mar) is the wrong lead tool against Beijing — China is only ~2% of U.S. steel imports after existing AD/CVD, while Canada, Brazil, Korea, Japan and the EU absorb the hit and have already threatened WTO cases and retaliation. Stacking an unfocused China package on top of that ally backlash would waste the one issue (IP/tech transfer) that has bipartisan and business support. A targeted 301 tariff list aimed at MIC 2025 products is the proportionate use of leverage after seven months of a completed investigation and a failed summit. Restraint below maximal escalation is required because China has already previewed farm-belt counters (sorghum AD/CVD after the Jan Section 201 solar/washer tariffs; ASA reports Beijing named soybeans — $12–14bn of U.S. exports — as a prime target, with Brazil as a ready substitute) and Lighthizer himself told Ways & Means on 21 Mar that Chinese retaliation is “inevitable.” Concede-purchases or rollback would cash in unused leverage for nothing; hold would ratify Beijing’s bet that Washington will blink. Calibrated 301 tariffs plus an open negotiating door is the action that matches a mild opportunity reading.
key_factors: Unresolved forced technology transfer, discriminatory licensing, state-directed tech acquisitions, and cyber IP theft after a 7-month 301 investigation and a no-concession Beijing summit
U.S. macro resilience (sentiment, industrial production, contained inflation) versus a still-large bilateral goods gap that gives Washington more goods-market leverage than Beijing
Section 232 steel/aluminum is poorly targeted at China (~2% of U.S. steel imports) and has already alienated the EU, Japan, and Korea whose support is needed on IP
China has previewed politically targeted farm retaliation (sorghum probe; soybeans named), so the 301 list must stay bounded and paired with a talks track
White House is already teed up for a Thursday 301 announcement in the $30–60bn range aimed at Made in China 2025; investment/visa measures are not ready and should stay in reserve

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump signs memorandum directing USTR to investigate China's IP and technology-transfer practices under Section 301. USTR investigation initiated.
Trump visits Beijing; large package of commercial deals announced (many MOUs). No substantive concessions on structural IP / tech-transfer issues.
Trump approves Section 201 safeguard tariffs on solar panels and washing machines (China among suppliers hit). First major tariff action of the administration.
Trump signs Section 232 proclamations imposing the steel (25%) and aluminum (10%) tariffs.
U.S. consumer sentiment 101.4 as of 2018-03-01 — expansion-high confidence, dispute not biting households yet.
U.S. industrial production 102.2067 (2017=100) in March 2018, up over the lookback window.
U.S. goods imports from China still ~$38.3bn in March 2018 versus exports to China of ~$12.7bn (EXPCH), a large bilateral imbalance.
China reserves ex-gold ~$3.16tn in March 2018, stable — no financial-stress signal that would make Beijing unable to absorb a calibrated tariff hit.

21 Mar 2018: White House set to announce 301 tariffs the next day; Lighthizer told Ways & Means retaliation is inevitable and the U.S. cannot take no action for fear of it; Trump has pushed toward ~$60bn while statute limits remedies to estimated harm.
14 Mar 2018: USTR drafted ~$30bn of China tariffs equal to estimated annual forced-transfer value; Trump wanted a higher number; list expected to hit Made in China 2025 products.
Commerce data: Chinese steel ~2% of U.S. steel imports by quantity (about 3.5% by value) after existing AD/CVD covering ~90% of Chinese steel.
China opened AD/CVD on U.S. sorghum (~$1bn, nearly all of China's sorghum imports) less than two weeks after U.S. solar/washer tariffs — a farm-belt political counter.
American Soybean Association: 'We have heard directly from the Chinese that U.S. soybeans are prime targets for retaliation'; China is not locked into U.S. supply.
USCBC 28 Sep 2017 301 submission: nearly 20% of companies asked to transfer technology in the past three years; JV/equity caps and opaque approvals are the pressure points.
15 Mar 2018 Covington: 301 has bipartisan support, but 232 steel/aluminum talks with EU/Japan crowded out coordination on China IP — ally cohesion is already fraying.
